section_summary: This section documents U.S. monitoring and control of strategic exports to Japan and Japanese-controlled territories, including petroleum, iron and steel, copper, cotton, machinery, and technical industrial information. It includes intelligence reports on German supplies entering Manchuria, fuel and metal shipments routed through China and the Americas, and suspected schemes to divert American aviation fuel to the Japanese Navy. A substantial policy sequence considers British proposals for coordinated economic restrictions, while other correspondence debates embargo strategy, export licensing, and the economic consequences for the Philippines and Latin American producers.

subfiles.title: Telegram on German machinery and military matériel entering Manchuria
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports German industrial and military equipment recently transported into Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Grew lists monthly arrivals from January through March, including coal-cutting machinery, Bosch magnetos, locomotives, trucks, aircraft and factory machinery, artillery tractors, torpedo boats, submarines, tools, and drilling equipment. The telegram was sent to the Department through Shanghai, and page 297 provides a substantially similar paraphrase with several OCR-corrupted quantities.

subfiles.title: Office of Production Management routing note concerning mineral production
subfiles.from: Office of Production Management, Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Transmits or comments on information concerning the production and availability of a strategic mineral, apparently cobalt.
subfiles.summary: Most of the text is obscured, but the surviving lines refer to production, possible supply, and countries producing cobalt. The sheet was received and filed by the Department of State in April 1941.

subfiles.title: War Department transmittal and intelligence report on Japanese merchant shipping
subfiles.doc_type: letter of transmittal with intelligence enclosure
subfiles.from: Sherman Miles, Military Intelligence Division, G-2
subfiles.to: A. A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards intelligence communications, including a report on Japanese insistence that pulp shipments move in Japanese vessels.
subfiles.summary: The covering letter lists four intelligence enclosures concerning individuals and Japanese merchant shipping. The surviving shipping report states that Japanese interests required pulp to be carried in Japanese bottoms, refused other arrangements, and then advised that no Japanese ships would be available in April and May, forcing another means of shipment.

subfiles.title: Recent arrivals of gasoline and diesel oil at Tsingtao on American ships
subfiles.from: Paul W. Meyer, American Consul, Tsingtao
subfiles.about: Reports large American-ship deliveries of gasoline and diesel fuel to Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha at Tsingtao.
subfiles.summary: The S.S. Scottsburg carried 37,904 drums of gasoline and 834 tons of diesel oil, bringing February gasoline arrivals for Mitsubishi to almost 3.71 million gallons. Because the cargoes were duty-free, handled at a military-restricted wharf, and commercially disproportionate, the consul presumed that they were intended for Japanese military and naval use. The despatch also discusses the crews' decision to remain aboard to avoid disputes with Japanese military sentries.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of constituent correspondence
subfiles.from: James M. Mead, United States Senate
subfiles.about: Refers an enclosed constituent communication for consideration and a report.
subfiles.summary: Senator Mead asks the State Department to give favorable consideration to the enclosed communication and return it with a report. The enclosure is Madeleine C. Curtis's letter on exports to the Axis through Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter protesting shipment of fats to the Far East
subfiles.from: Madeleine C. Curtis
subfiles.about: Questions why the United States permits fats and other goods to be shipped toward Japan when they may ultimately aid Germany.
subfiles.summary: Curtis cites reports that one hundred railcars of fat were moving from Chicago to the Pacific Coast and that Germany had seized Italian olive oil. She argues that supplying Axis needs through the Pacific undermines efforts to assist Britain in the Atlantic and asks why the traffic is not stopped.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Mead concerning war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains the licensing controls applied to fats, oils, and other exports that might aid Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that animal and vegetable fats and oils require special export licenses and that licenses are withheld when proposed exports would harm national defense. It adds that export controls are continually adjusted, with licenses refused and new commodities added whenever changing conditions warrant.

subfiles.title: Summary of the Universal Oil Products–Japan Gasoline Company case
subfiles.from: H. W. Moseley, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Reviews litigation and export-license issues involving American petroleum-process information sought by a Japanese company.
subfiles.summary: Japan Gasoline Company sued Universal Oil Products after the American firm stopped performing contracts for motor- and aviation-gasoline technology following the moral embargo. The Department allowed work under the 1928 motor-gasoline contract but rejected licenses for technical information under the 1938 aviation contract. The Japanese Embassy proposed settling the suit if some processes were licensed, but H. J. Halle reported that the requested information also covered toluene and synthetic rubber and that he did not wish to provide it.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on proposed Haitian cotton barter with Japan
subfiles.from: Division of the American Republics
subfiles.about: Summarizes reports that a Haitian cotton sale to Japan may include tariff concessions for Japanese textiles.
subfiles.summary: Minister White reports that the cotton transaction may be a barter arrangement admitting Japanese cotton goods at minimum tariff rates. Officials consider whether British or Canadian purchasers might instead buy the cotton and whether the matter should be discussed with President-elect Lescot or M. Dennis while they are in Washington.

subfiles.title: Sale of Haitian cotton to Japan
subfiles.from: John Campbell White, American Legation, Port-au-Prince
subfiles.about: Reports negotiations to sell Haitian cotton to Japanese interests through a possible barter and tariff arrangement.
subfiles.summary: Pixley said that Mansour had bought or taken options on cotton for Japanese interests and sought minimum-tariff entry for Japanese cotton goods in return. White recognized Haiti's urgent need for export markets but suggested approaching the British purchasing agent and Canadian Legation. The contemplated quantity was about 1,500 tons, to be shipped through New York and transferred to a Japanese vessel after passing through the Panama Canal.

subfiles.title: Instruction opposing a Haitian barter arrangement with Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Authorizes the Legation to discourage Haiti from exchanging cotton for Japanese manufactures.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Haiti's need to find a market for its cotton. It nevertheless states that, given the international situation and possible consequences, the United States would regret a Haitian barter arrangement involving Japanese manufactured goods.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of information obtained by the Canadian censor
subfiles.from: Edward T. Wailes, Division of European Affairs
subfiles.about: Forwards an informal memorandum based on information intercepted by Canadian censorship.
subfiles.summary: Wailes records that an officer of the Canadian Legation informally supplied the attached memorandum. The attachment concerns an individual's claims about gasoline unloaded in Japan and brass moving through Vladivostok to Germany.

subfiles.title: Extract from censored letter on gasoline and brass shipments
subfiles.from: Canadian censorship source
subfiles.about: Quotes a letter from Kobe describing gasoline deliveries to Japan and brass allegedly routed to Germany.
subfiles.summary: A writer in Kobe tells Vera Tinker that his ship unloaded gasoline for three days at Itasaki despite an apparent embargo. He also says brass was being unloaded at Kobe for movement through Vladivostok to Germany for ammunition manufacture and notes an expected arrival at San Pedro on December 15.

subfiles.title: California Texas Oil Company report of petroleum shipments from Bahrain
subfiles.from: W. H. Pinckard, California Texas Oil Company, Limited
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Department of State
subfiles.about: Supplies a table of company petroleum cargoes shipped from Bahrain to Japan and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure lists four tanker cargoes loaded at Bahrain during September through November and discharged at Kure or Dairen. The products include diesel oil and gasoline consigned to Manshu Sekiyu Kaisha or the Texas Company's China affiliate, totaling roughly 307,688 barrels.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of California Texas Oil Company shipment data
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of petroleum-shipment information and offers to meet Pinckard in Washington.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Pinckard for his February 8 letter and enclosure on shipments from Bahrain to Japan and Manchuria. He says he would be glad to see Pinckard during a future visit to Washington.

subfiles.title: Telegram on a Paraguayan cotton negotiation with Japan
subfiles.from: Norman Armour
subfiles.about: Reports negotiations involving the Paraguayan government and a proposed cotton transaction with Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: A trustworthy source reports that the Paraguayan government is negotiating an agreement concerning cotton. The discussed price appears to be about 300 pesos per metric ton, c.i.f. Buenos Aires, payable in Argentine pesos in Asunción; the information was repeated to Asunción with a suggestion that Pearson be informed.

subfiles.title: Cover letter forwarding Julian Randolph's embargo proposals
subfiles.from: Roger S. Greene, Committee to Defend America by Aiding the Allies
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards a University of California economist's letter advocating stronger restrictions on trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greene sends Julian Randolph's letter because of its potential interest to Far Eastern affairs officials. He notes growing concern that the United States continues supplying Japan with materials also needed for American defense and emphasizes Randolph's distinction between goods available to Japan in Asia and other war materials.

subfiles.title: Julian Randolph letter advocating a selective but stringent embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: Julian Randolph
subfiles.about: Argues that a selective embargo could restrain Japanese expansion while reducing the likelihood of a Pacific war.
subfiles.summary: Randolph argues that aiding Britain and confronting Japanese expansion are equally urgent because Japan seeks control of Southeast Asian rubber, tin, oil, and Philippine iron ore. He recommends exempting petroleum, iron ore, rubber, and tin from embargo while imposing an airtight prohibition on other war materials that Japan cannot readily obtain elsewhere. He contends that a decisive embargo would weaken Japan's war machine, preserve American naval freedom for the Atlantic, and give Ambassador Nomura a basis for rebuilding peaceful Japanese-American relations.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Greene's letter and Randolph enclosure
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Thanks Greene for forwarding Randolph's embargo recommendations.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges Greene's February 12 letter and the enclosed February 4 letter from Julian Randolph. He notes that Randolph has already supplied the Department with several memoranda on restrictions on trade with Japan but appreciates receiving the additional copy.

subfiles.title: Controls note on licensing re-export through New York
subfiles.from: Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Records arrangements to require a license before the cargo under discussion can be re-exported through New York.
subfiles.summary: The short handwritten note states that arrangements have been made to require a license before the material can be re-exported from New York. In context, it appears to concern the copper shipment later described in the Panama Canal intelligence report.

subfiles.title: American Republics Division note requesting information on copper bound for Japan
subfiles.from: Division of the American Republics
subfiles.about: Refers an earlier departmental request for information concerning a copper shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The brief note asks the Controls desk to consult an earlier Department communication requesting information about copper destined for Japan. Its placement associates it with the S.S. Biancamano shipment routed through New York.

subfiles.title: Military intelligence report on copper removed from the S.S. Biancamano
subfiles.doc_type: intelligence report with distribution sheet and duplicate copy
subfiles.from: L. D. Carter, G-2, Panama Canal Department
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Describes copper sold at Cristóbal and routed in bond through New York for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The report lists lots scheduled aboard the S.S. Cristobal, S.S. Ancon, and S.S. Panama for delivery to New York. Bills of lading were to identify the cargo as in transit for a Japanese firm in Osaka, with Florencio E. Delgado acting locally and H. S. Dorf handling New York arrangements. Carter notes that the circuitous routing was not understood and that local inquiries had not established its purpose.

subfiles.title: American aviation gasoline to be bootlegged to the Japanese Navy
subfiles.from: Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.to: Naval and State Department intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: Reports an alleged scheme to obtain American aviation fuel under cover of deliveries to the Chungking government.
subfiles.summary: Documents attributed to the German Ulrich Fuel Company describe a plan for R. S. Boyd's North American Syndicate to buy aviation gasoline in the United States ostensibly for China. Japanese authorities would allow about twenty percent to reach Chungking while confiscating the remaining eighty percent for Japanese use. A proposed contract covered aviation gasoline, aviation lubricants, and diesel oil for the Japanese Navy through intermediary firms.

subfiles.title: Memorandum placing Japanese oil-export licenses in statistical perspective
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Adds comparative figures to data on licenses for gasoline and crude-oil exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum converts the licensing figures to standard forty-two-gallon barrels so they can be compared consistently. It also reports Charles Yost's view that prohibiting drum exports should sharply reduce gasoline shipments because tanker space was scarce and gasoline was difficult to handle in tankers.

subfiles.title: Dominican customs circular prohibiting export of scrap iron
subfiles.from: Thomas Pearson, Deputy Receiver General
subfiles.about: Orders Dominican customs offices not to permit scrap-iron exports without prior authorization.
subfiles.summary: The circular implements instructions from the Dominican Secretariat of the Treasury and Commerce. From February 25 onward, scrap iron could not be exported unless the Secretariat had first approved the shipment.

subfiles.title: Reply to Lindley Beckworth on scrap exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Explains that iron and steel scrap exports to Japan were barred under the licensing policy announced in September 1940.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Beckworth's inquiry about whether scrap shipments to Japan remain permissible. He states that, effective October 16, licenses would not be issued for scrap shipments outside the Western Hemisphere and Great Britain and encloses the pertinent presidential press release.

subfiles.title: Conversation with British Embassy officers on trade restrictions and oil for Japan
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Records British pressure for action on coordinated trade restrictions and Japanese accumulation of petroleum.
subfiles.summary: G. F. Thorold and P. C. Hill sought a prompt response to British memoranda proposing cooperation on trade restrictions and measures against excessive Japanese oil stocks. They wanted progress before negotiations between Japanese representatives and the Netherlands East Indies were concluded. Thorold also submitted a paper showing that Persian Gulf petroleum shipments had been small in both absolute and comparative terms.

subfiles.title: Political Relations memorandum urging senior review of the British proposals
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Ray Atherton, and Dean Acheson
subfiles.about: Frames the Japanese-supply problem as part of broader American defense policy rather than solely a Far Eastern or European matter.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that the file concerns relations with both Britain and Japan as well as the larger problem of implementing national-defense policy. It advises officers who may attend a conference contemplated by Sumner Welles and the Secretary to study the file and prepare to discuss the British recommendations and proposed alternatives.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary's note postponing further consideration
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Recommends delaying action on the British economic-policy proposals until the Secretary returns.
subfiles.summary: Welles states that he has reviewed the papers and believes further consideration should wait. Because the Secretary had been personally involved in the matter, Welles considered it wiser not to proceed in his absence.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs views on machinery for restricting exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Supports limiting Japanese imports to normal quantities but questions the need for a broad new interdepartmental organization.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum favors steps to restrict exports to Japan to normal quantities while continuing existing information exchanges with Britain and using established agencies. It would make an exception for petroleum, whose complexity might justify a special interdepartmental committee. It also stresses that decisions on trade with Japan are fundamentally questions of foreign relations.

subfiles.title: Consideration of United States policy toward Japan's acquisition of war materials
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.to: Secretary of State and senior policy officials
subfiles.about: Analyzes British proposals for coordinated measures to prevent Japan from accumulating excessive stocks of war materials.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes Britain's argument that Japan's stockpiling reduces democratic leverage and may permit Japan to choose the most advantageous moment for war. It evaluates export controls, shipping restrictions, preemptive purchasing in South America, limits on imports from Japan, and specialized machinery for petroleum policy. It recommends accepting the British proposals in principle, creating an interdepartmental committee under Dean Acheson, and establishing a small State Department unit to analyze petroleum exports and recommend controls.

subfiles.title: Foreign Funds Control procedure for exports to Japan and Manchuria
subfiles.from: Foreign Funds Control
subfiles.about: Sets interim rules for handling applications to export goods to Japan after the freezing order.
subfiles.summary: Foreign Funds Control would deny most controlled merchandise and strategic categories, including wood pulp, metals, machinery, rubber, and chemicals, while petroleum required an export license. Cotton and miscellaneous applications were to be held pending policy decisions, as were Latin American exports financed through blocked Japanese accounts. The memorandum also notes general licenses for trade with non-Manchurian China and between the Philippines, China, and Japan.

subfiles.title: Iron ore exports from the Philippines to Japan
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Assesses Philippine and Malayan iron-ore quotas and the effects of a complete embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost compares Philippine export quotas with British restrictions on Malayan ore and concludes that the two countries were following roughly parallel courses. A combined embargo on ore and Indian pig iron might reduce Japan's available iron supplies by about one quarter. He warns, however, that a complete embargo would close the four Philippine mines and therefore require federal relief for those affected.

subfiles.title: Department of Commerce communication on foreign-trade information
subfiles.from: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, Division of Foreign Trade Statistics
subfiles.about: Transmits or responds to a request for foreign-trade statistical information; much of the text is illegible.
subfiles.summary: The surviving letterhead and signature identify the Department of Commerce's foreign-trade statistics office. The substantive lines are too damaged to recover reliably, but the communication was received by the State Department in mid-March and filed with the Japan export-control material.

subfiles.title: Explanation of iron and steel licensing policy for Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Explains how the presidential 'usual or pre-war' formula is applied to iron and steel exports to Japan and occupied China.
subfiles.summary: Green states that nearly all iron and steel products may be licensed to Japan and Japanese-occupied China in quantities based on 1935–1936 trade. Scarce types required for American defense, Britain, or the American republics receive smaller allocations. He denies that this explanation conflicts with statements made by Price and DeGolia; pages 365–366 duplicate the memorandum.

subfiles.title: Request for Controls comment on conflicting accounts of steel-export practice
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Requests clarification after earlier memoranda suggested that Japan was not actually receiving normal prewar quantities of steel products.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton notes Green's assertion that the usual-or-prewar formula governs iron and steel manufactures. He contrasts that position with two Adams memoranda indicating that shipments to Japan and occupied China were below normal and asks Green to comment. Page 368 is a Division of Controls separator or continuation sheet associated with the referral.

subfiles.title: Inquiry whether the prewar formula governs iron and steel exports
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Seeks confirmation that the usual-or-prewar formula still applies to iron and steel exports to Japan and occupied China.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton recalls that he and Hornbeck strongly supported the formula when iron and steel manufactures were placed under control. Although he understands that it remains in force, he asks Green to confirm that interpretation after the issue was raised internally.

subfiles.title: Adams memorandum on priorities governing iron and steel export licenses
subfiles.from: Mr. Adams, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Reports how defense, British, hemispheric, and friendly-country priorities affect steel exports to Japan and occupied China.
subfiles.summary: Price described a priority order placing American defense first, followed by Britain and its allies, the Western Hemisphere, and then friendly countries sharing any surplus. Free China was treated with Britain, while occupied China was generally treated like Japan. DeGolia added that steel applications for occupied China required individual review, and Adams saw no proper basis to stop a particular shipment if it did not legally constitute scrap.

subfiles.title: Adams follow-up on actual application of the prewar formula
subfiles.from: Mr. Adams, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Clarifies that the usual-or-prewar formula applies only after higher-priority demands have been satisfied.
subfiles.summary: Price told Adams that his statement and Green's were not formally inconsistent. In practice, however, shortages in many controlled commodities meant that Japan and occupied China were receiving far less than normal quantities despite the nominal formula.

subfiles.title: British request for consultation before further petroleum restrictions
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Records a British Embassy request to be consulted before the United States adopts new petroleum-export restrictions affecting Japan.
subfiles.summary: J. S. Dent said the Embassy understood that further petroleum restrictions, especially against Japan, were under consideration and hoped to be consulted before a decision. He reported Dutch concern that new restrictions could disrupt negotiations to renew the Netherlands Indies oil agreement expiring May 1. Yost assured Dent that he would keep him informed.

subfiles.title: War Department transmittal of intelligence on the S.S. Biancamano copper shipment
subfiles.from: Sherman Miles, Military Intelligence Division, G-2
subfiles.to: A. A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards a military-intelligence summary concerning copper removed from the S.S. Biancamano.
subfiles.summary: Miles sends the intelligence communication for the Department's information and any action considered advisable. The listed enclosure is a March 5 summary concerning the Biancamano copper shipment; the enclosure itself falls beyond this section.
